Another problem that I've noticed with sci-fi television and movies is that they're made to appeal to the masses in a way that didn't used to happen. Even some of the great things to come out of the genre recently, like Interstellar, were so dumbed down and full of exposition that they missed a great opportunity to showcase the world around them.

It's like the movie Her - the world was was a spectacle, but they spent the whole time on a generic love story (unlike Farscape) - occasionally showcasing this and that. Why bother creating your world and imagine the possibilities in that world if you're not going to explore it with the viewers? The best sci-fi lets the world dictate the story, not the other way around - and hopefully doesn't make the mistake of trying to explain every last detail of that world. The unknown can be just as impactful as the known. This is a fact that makes Fury Road a good movie (though I still don't think it was one of the "best actions films ever" as seems to be opined here and there.)

I basically avoid all big television Sci-Fi. The fantasy genre, I think, is still doing pretty well; but it seems like these day the only thing you get out of big sci-fi television is either yet another cop drama, or yet another zombie drama. I have always, and even more so now, hated zombies - with the important exception of 28 Days Later. That movie was great because it's a mystery to you and to the character - you discover the world together.

There's a lot of compelling stuff coming out of the smaller scale sci-fi television shows, though. I think that Netflix support really helps bring out some gems that network TV finds too risky. I really enjoyed Sense8. It was certainly unique, but it also took the thing that made it different and built it into the story well. Black Mirror is probably the finest example of drop-you-into-the-world sci-fi. And if you haven't seen it, watch it. And of course I like a lot of the space opera sci-fi. Farscape is my favorite show of all time. It's one of those shows that has just enough fantasy (or, I guess, the fi part of sci-fi.) and it's not afraid to really throw some crazy shit at you; (John Quixote, anyone?)

As much as I love the space opera's though, I always get really excited about more terrestrial sci-fi. And I don't mean "look at our fancy computers in an otherwise unremarkable today-like world" I mean some real "what if things were like this?" But no more zombies. No more post-apocalypse survival (unless it offers something truely unique; Mad Max 1, 2, and 4) No more crime shows. Just no more drama unless you really know what you're doing in sci-fi; Battlestar Galactica and SGU. And for the love of god, I am so done with super heroes. None of them are as good as The Dark Knight.

To address some of your points; I agree that there's no good excuse for getting the trivial things wrong. There's no need to have explanations for every little detail, but come on - we all know how rust works. However, there are times when they actually did get it right, but it's just not something that seems correct. I think, though, that the star thing is a little too nit picky. I think most people would speak that way - They know that the person was assuming it was a star, so it's more intuitively identifiable. And I wholly agree about the sci-fi writers part. Though I think what's more important is to have a variety of people to bounce ideas around with.
